title: The Beverly Hills Supper Club Fire
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the 1977 Beverly Hills Supper Club fire in Southgate, Kentucky, near Newport and Cincinnati, which killed 165 people. The episode traces Northern Kentucky's Prohibition-era bootlegging under George Remus, the Cleveland mob led by Moe Dalitz (spelled "Deletes" in the transcript), and Newport's reputation as a gambling and vice capital. It covers the 1961 sheriff election of George Radermann and the federal crackdown that followed, then the club's history under Dick Schilling, who reopened it in 1971 after earlier fires. The episode describes the Memorial Day weekend 1977 night when John Davidson was headlining, the fire that began in the Zebra Room, busboy Walter Bailey's calm evacuation announcement, and the blocked cabaret room exit. It also covers the disputed cause (officially undetermined; aluminum wiring was blamed initially and a grand jury found code violations), arson theories, the lawsuit, and later redevelopment of the site. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about avocado toast and hamburger steak and a brief outro.

segments.title: Introduction to the Beverly Hills Supper Club fire
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode on the 1977 Beverly Hills Supper Club fire, which killed 165 people and was a national news event. He and Chuck note they knew little about it before researching.

segments.title: Prohibition bootlegging and George Remus
segments.summary: Northern Kentucky's Prohibition-era liquor trade is described, including the medicinal whiskey loophole in the Volstead Act. George Remus, a Chicago lawyer and pharmacist, moved to Cincinnati to run a bootlegging empire, earning huge sums. His later shooting of his wife Imogene and his insanity acquittal are covered.

segments.title: Newport as a gambling town and the Cleveland mob
segments.summary: Newport became a vice town with a red light district. Peter Man (spelled Peachman in the transcript) bought the Beverly Hills roadhouse in 1937 and turned it into a carpet joint casino. The Cleveland mob led by Moe Dalitz took over Newport, which was called Sin City. Dalitz later helped found Las Vegas.

segments.title: Newport's heyday and the federal crackdown
segments.summary: Newport drew large weekend crowds and celebrity performers while operating in a state without legal gambling. The Kefauver Committee hearings in 1950 failed to shut it down. A 1957 meeting of mob bosses in Appalachin, New York changed federal views on organized crime. Newport's homicide rate and the 'Newport nightgown' killings are described.

segments.title: George Radermann sheriff election and the frame-up
segments.summary: Former Notre Dame and Browns player George Radermann ran for sheriff in 1961 as a reform candidate. He was found drugged and naked with a sex worker in a hotel room, and blood tests showed chloral hydrate. He won the election anyway, and Attorney General Robert Kennedy sent federal agents to Newport, ending its heyday in the 1960s.

segments.title: Dick Schilling and the club's rebuilding
segments.summary: After the club closed in the mid-1960s, Dick Schilling Jr. bought the abandoned property in 1969 and renamed it the Beverly Hills Supper Club. He restored it, a previous burning was attributed to mob pressure, and the club reopened in 1971 with performers such as Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, and the Righteous Brothers. Sources disagree about overcrowding.

segments.title: Sources and the Memorial Day 1977 night
segments.summary: The hosts cite books by Peter Bronson and Robert Webster and describe their feud. They set the scene on Memorial Day weekend 1977, when John Davidson was headlining with comedy openers Teeter and McDonald. About 3,000 people were in the complex, with several wedding parties.

segments.title: The fire, evacuation, and blocked exits
segments.summary: The fire starts in the Zebra Room after a wedding party leaves, and spreads up the hall of mirrors toward the Cabaret Room. Rick Schilling tries to fight it with an extinguisher. A busboy opens a door, which feeds the fire. Walter Bailey, a teenage busboy, calmly announces an evacuation from the stage. People are trapped at a single blocked exit and in dead-end hallways and a closet, and some die on the lawn. About 20 people escape. Survivors and the dead are described; the blaze burned for seven hours.

segments.title: Aftermath, investigations, and arson theories
segments.summary: Survivors and first responders are described. The site was used as a temporary morgue at the National Armory. Six investigations followed, and the initial finding blamed aluminum wiring. The Zebra Room was bulldozed the next day. A grand jury found the owner violated the fire code but not criminally. Authors suggest arson by the mob, citing tips, a prior explosion, and timers; the cause is officially undetermined.

segments.title: Lawsuit and the site today
segments.summary: Stan Chesley led a class action suit against the aluminum wiring industry, and families received about $30 million. The site in Southgate was later sold to a developer, and lawsuits followed over construction plans. Remains and artifacts are reportedly still on the land.

segments.title: Listener mail: avocado toast and hamburger steak
segments.summary: A listener writes that her father served avocado toast for decades and mentions growing up in San Diego. The hosts discuss hamburger steak, Kenji Lopez-Alt's recipes, and Sally's Baking Addiction cookies.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners and give the email address for mail.
